result:
The proposed answer of ∞ is incorrect. The claim that a C_{2k+1}-free graph with linear minimum degree must have odd girth above 2k+1 is false, and the whole infinite family 2/(2k+3) rests on it.

**Counterexample for C₅.** Take a triangle xyz. Attach each of x, y, z to one side of its own separate complete bipartite graph K_{m,m}, with x joined to every vertex of that side.

- The graph is non-bipartite because of the triangle.
- Every cycle lies inside a single block. The blocks are the triangle and the bipartite pieces, so the only odd cycle is the triangle. The graph is therefore C₅-free.
- The minimum degree is linear in n, roughly n/6 or more.

So δ_χ(C₅,2) is bounded below by a positive constant that is not 2/7. The same kind of construction works for longer odd cycles, which breaks the proposed formula 2/(g(H)+2).

**What I recall of the true result.** I am relying on memory here, not a derivation. Illingworth's work on minimum degree stability of H-free graphs shows that δ_χ(H,2) takes only finitely many values for 3-chromatic H. I recall the set as {1/3, 2/5, 1/2}, possibly with additional small values such as 0. Under that recollection the sum is finite, for example 1/3 + 2/5 + 1/2 = 37/30. I did not verify the exact set. Either way, the sum is not ∞.

VERDICT: REJECT
